The judge made this observation in the context of remarks on alternative dispute resolution (ADR) mechanisms. The Bar & Bench report captures his position that mandatory mediation, rather than encouraging settlement, can create friction and resistance among parties who have not voluntarily agreed to the process. Justice Bhambhani's comments reflect a judicial perspective that mediation works best when both parties enter the process willingly and in good faith, rather than under court compulsion. The statement appears part of broader judicial commentary on how courts should approach ADR in India, particularly relevant as Indian courts increasingly attempt to decongest dockets through mediation protocols under the Civil Procedure Code and court-annexed mediation schemes.
legal.contextNote: This reflects judicial resistance to mandatory mediation protocols introduced under the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (amendments enabling court-annexed mediation) and Mediation Act, 2023 framework. Justice Bhambhani's view directly challenges the Supreme Court's push post-*Natarajan v. Natarajan* (2018) toward pre-litigation and court-mandated ADR. In-house counsel should note: (1) Do not assume court-ordered mediation will settle; prepare litigation readiness even after ADR orders; (2) Track whether this Bombay High Court position influences other benches or invites Supreme Court clarification on the scope of mandatory mediation under new rules; (3) When advising clients on settlement strategy, distinguish between voluntary settlement conferences (likely to succeed per this reasoning) and imposed mediation (flagged here as friction-prone)—structure your pre-suit engagement accordingly.

retail.headline: FMCG distributors seek zero-MDR for UPI transactions; write to PM

world.summary: Russia is conducting parliamentary elections in four regions of Ukraine—Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia—that it annexed in 2022, despite widespread international condemnation.
